Zakaria Hossain Chowdhury ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Sabrina Choudhury and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
11. This matter has appeared in the cause list on 9-7-2017 for further hearing. The learned Advocate Mr Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Chowdhury, for the petitioner, having placed an affidavit-in-reply, dated 6-7-2017 (submitted on 9-7-2017), filed on behalf of the petitioner, refers to some notes of approval of Noorani Group, respectively dated 4-1-2014 (Annexure-N), dated 19-4-2014 (Annexure:N-1), dated 4-4-2014 (Annexure: N-3), salary increment statement (Annexure-O), and another note of approval dated 19-5-2014 and then submits that these and other documents annexed to this reply would show that the DMD (Respondent No. 1) and the CEO have been independently running and managing the affairs of the Noorani Group by giving necessary instructions and approvals and even by approving cost and expenses. Therefore, he emphasis that, clearly the employees who are said to be dealing with the CBL were all acting under the instruction and direction of the DMD (Respondent No. 1), not under the Managing Director (petitioner), who was then staying in London for treatment. He further submits that in paragraph No. 16 of the bank's affidavit-in-opposition, it has been admitted that, the petitioner habitually submits documents by scanning or photocopying from the same source through his employee, the said M. Shamsul Alam Bahiyan, when he remains out of the country. He therefore emphatically argues that, as admitted by the Bank, the petitioner himself did not put his signature on Form III(A), and that the signatures appearing on the DRF and other letters including the application dated 7-5-2014 for approval to gifting shares (Annexure-C) were put by scanning during his (petitioner's) absence. Therefore, the learned Advocate was very serious in urging upon the Court to take legal action against the concerned officials of the bank alleging that the bank has acted without exercising due diligence and had verified the signature of the petitioner though it was not original according to their knowledge and the so-called verification of a signature on Form No. III(A) was done even without making any query with the petitioner, though it involved a huge number of shares. Appeared at this stage, as Senior Advocate for the petitioner, Mr Akhtar Imam continued the submission, with leave of the Court, that once the petitioner has denied his signature, on the application, dated 7-5-2014, for approval of gifting shares in Form III(A) to the petition (Annexure-C), then the burden of proof shifts and lies upon the Respondent No. 1 to prove that the petitioner had in fact made a gift of the disputed shares in her favour and that the signature appearing on Form III(A) for approval of the gift is the signature of the petitioner. He has relied upon an unreported judgment, passed in Civil Revision No. 1443 of 2008, wherein in a case concerning a dispute regarding payment of rent between the landlord and the tenant, if has been held that, once the landlord has denied to have received the rent, the duty to prove payment of the rent has been shifted to the other side i.e. upon the tenant. Learned Advocate Mr Kazi Akter Hamid, also in the relay, at the last stage, stood for the petitioner. He submits that the process of gift of the disputed shares has not been done in accordance with law and if the petitioner had any intention to make a gift of his shares then he would have ratified all these acts in writing or otherwise, but there is no such proof that the petitioner had even ratified or intended to ratify the disputed transfer by way of gift, while his clear case is that he did not make any gift of his shares to Respondent No. 1. 

 12. Learned Advocate Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, in reply submits that, the gift of shares was done voluntarily and as willed by the petitioner. But for his instruction or consent, the learned Advocate continues, no one would have acted on the instruction of the Respondent No. 1. Indeed, he proceeds on that, the Respondent No. 1 was also in London during the relevant period and she did not orchestrate the transfer of shares, from London, as alleged. There is no proof either to make such a wild allegation against Respondent No. 1. It is the petitioner who did everything to give effect to the transfer of his shares and in the manner devised by him. Hence, he (the petitioner) did not question the change in the register of members or in respect of payment of dividend, for quite a long time. He concludes that transfer of 2,77,00,000 numbers of shares to respondent No. 1, who is his spouse and mother of their two children, was done properly. So, this is not a fit case for allowing by this Court. 

 25. It is also to be noted here that, the question of apparent similarity between the signatures appearing on the DRF and on Form III(A) is not the issue in this case. The issue is, whether the petitioner himself had put any signature on the Form No. III(A) dated 7-5-2014 (Annexure-C), which is a legally mandatory requirement for making a gift of the shares of a public company listed with the exchange. Even the theory that the petitioner usually deals with his shares through a scanning his signature will, in no way, help improving the case of the respondent No. 1, because the request for approval of the gift of share must be based and considered on the original signature of the petitioner, to be put on Form III(A), and nothing less then that can constitute any valid gift or confer any valid title in the disputed shares, moreso, in the absence of any proof of gift, as distinct from unapproval for gift. Any deviation from this will no; only be illegal, rather it will open a floodgate for doing fraud and forgery in the hands of unscrupulous officials or persons at various level. 

 26. Therefore, these factual issues, based on the preponderance of the evidence, clearly prove that the petitioner himself did not sign the application dated 7-5-2014 (Annexure-C) in Form III(A) for approval of gifting his 2,77,00,000 shares, nor he had taken any decision to pay service charge on 19-5-2014 for transferring the disputed shares was taken by him, nor he had any intention to make the questioned gift, nor was it possible on his part to do the alleged act, done during his absence from 4-1-2014 to 23-7-2014. In consequence, the burden to prove that the petitioner had gifted the shares and other relevant facts, that has been shifted to and rested upon the respondent No. 1, could not be discharged by her. Even, as per section 103 of the Evidence Act, 1872, the burden that rests upon the Respondent No. 1, she has failed to discharge that as well.
